skill.name: Then and now: what a text shows about the time it was written
skill.why: Old texts are time machines. They show how people lived and thought.
skill.how: Notice what the writer treats as normal. Ask: is that still true now?

beats.say: Every text is written at a certain time.
It shows what was normal back then.
beats.show: School rules, 1952: **All boys must wear a cap and tie.**

beats.say: The writer doesn't explain it. Everyone just did it.
Now compare it with today. Is it still the same?
Different? Then the text shows how times have changed.

creature.name: Thennit
creature.blurb: A hermit crab that lives in old things the tide brings back: a tin lunchbox, a teacup, an inkwell. Each shell shows it how people used to live.

encounters.frame: The Thennit crawled out of an old school bag. A letter was stuck to its shell.
encounters.text: Twotide School. 3 February 1955. Dear Parents, School starts again on Monday. Boys must wear a grey shirt and a tie. Girls must wear a dress and a hat. Every child needs a slate and a stick of chalk. There is no school canteen, so please send a cut lunch. Children must walk to school or ride a bike. Children who are late will stand at the back of the room. Yours sincerely, Miss Pratt, Head Teacher
encounters.prompt: What does this letter show about school in 1955?
encounters.success: Slates, chalk and cut lunches. The letter shows school in 1955 was very different from now.

options.text: Girls and boys wore the same uniform.
options.reason: Boys wore a shirt and tie. Girls wore a dress and a hat.

options.text: Children wrote on slates, and there was no canteen.
Parents drove their kids to school in the family car.
options.reason: The letter says children must walk or ride a bike.

encounters.frame: The Thennit found a letter in an old ink bottle. Gus says the girl who wrote it would have loved his gadgets.
encounters.text: Hartwell School, 12 May 1908. Dearest Papa, I am trying to be good, but it is very hard. Every afternoon, the boys go into the big room for science. They are building a steam engine out of a kettle! The girls go into the small room for needlework. Miss Hale says that sewing is what young ladies need, because one day we will run a household. Today I asked if I could join the boys, just for one lesson. Miss Hale went pale and said, 'Certainly not, Florence. Science is not for girls.' So I sewed a handkerchief instead. It has a steam engine on it. Please, Papa, may I have a book about engines for my birthday? Your loving daughter, Florence.
encounters.prompt: What does Florence's letter show about life for girls in 1908?
encounters.success: Her teacher says science is not for girls. In 1908, girls were taught sewing to run a household.

options.text: Girls could choose any subject they liked.
options.reason: Florence asks to join science and is told 'Certainly not'.

options.text: Girls were expected to learn sewing, not science.
Boys and girls learnt every subject together in the same room.
options.reason: The boys go to the big room for science. The girls go to a different room.

encounters.frame: The second tide brought the Thennit home in an old lantern. A letter was folded inside.
encounters.text: Gull Point, 20 June 1934. Dear Mum, The boats left on Tuesday morning and won't be back until Friday night. Once they sail past the point, there is no way to send them a message, so all we can do is wait. Every night, Gran puts a lamp in the front window, so Dad can find his way home in the dark. When the wind gets up, the whole village goes down to the jetty and stares at the sea. Nobody says much. The children are not allowed to play on the rocks while the boats are out, in case the waves come up. On Friday, the first person to see the sails rings the church bell, and everybody runs. Your loving daughter, Maggie.

encounters.frame: The Thennit is living in an old television knob. It brought a newspaper with it.
encounters.text: TWOTIDE TIMES, 9 August 1958. TELEVISION COMES TO THE ISLAND. Twotide Atoll has its first television sets. Only three houses on the island have one so far, and Mr Hooper's electrical shop has a fourth set in its front window. Every afternoon, crowds of children press their noses against the glass to watch cartoons, even though they cannot hear a sound. Mr Hooper says the pictures travel all the way from the mainland through the air, though nobody on the island quite understands how. Not everyone is pleased. Dr Fenwick warned parents this week that children who sit closer than two metres to the screen may damage their eyes. 'Some children are watching for an hour a day,' he said. 'That cannot be good for them.' The Reverend Platt worried that families would stop talking to each other at dinner. Mrs Hooper, however, said television was 'a marvel', and that her husband had sold eleven aerials in a week. The island council will meet on Tuesday to decide whether television should be allowed on Sundays.

encounters.frame: The Thennit is living in an old jelly mould. Mo found a household guide underneath it.
encounters.text: From The Twotide Household Guide, 1952. Keeping a Happy Home. Every Tuesday, the iceman delivers a fresh block of ice for the ice chest, so be sure to leave the side gate open. If the ice chest begins to smell, scrub it out with bicarbonate of soda. Each morning before dawn, the milkman brings the milk by horse and cart, so leave the empty bottles on the front step. Store leftover meat in a covered dish inside the ice chest. Sweep the front step every morning, so the neighbours can see that yours is a tidy house. Always wash your hands before you start to cook. Our street has no electric light yet, so fill the kerosene lamps before it gets dark. Never leave a hot pan where small children can reach it. Teach children to say please and thank you at the table. On washing day, which is Monday, light the copper early, because the sheets will take all morning to boil.
encounters.prompt: Is each piece of 1952 advice different now, or still the same?
encounters.success: Safety and manners haven't changed. Ice deliveries, kerosene lamps and coppers show 1952's ways.

items.reason: Today, fridges keep food cold. Nobody needs ice delivered.

items.reason: This is still the first rule of cooking today.

items.text: The milkman brings the milk by horse and cart.
items.reason: Today, milk comes from the shop. No horse and cart brings it to your step.

items.text: Fill the kerosene lamps before it gets dark.
items.reason: Today, homes have electric lights. Nobody fills a lamp to see at night.

encounters.text: Mars Academy, Year 6 History. Lesson notes, 4 March 2350. Today we learned about the strange old days of the 2020s, and honestly, some of it was hard to believe. People back then steered their own cars with their hands, and they had to stop at red lights, even when nobody was coming. Our cars drive themselves, so we just tell them where to go and read a book. encounters.frame: The Thennit found a letter inside an old wooden box. Wren went very quiet when she read it.
encounters.text: Elm Cottage, 2 November 1895. Dear Uncle Henry, I have wonderful news. My collection of birds' eggs now has forty-one eggs in it, all taken from nests in the bush behind the school this spring. I keep them in a wooden box lined with cotton wool, each with a little label. Last Saturday I climbed to the very top of a gum tree for a magpie's egg. The magpie was not pleased and pecked my ear, but I got the egg. Mr Lister, our teacher, says that collecting eggs teaches a boy patience and a love of nature, and he has given me a prize for the best collection in the school. Father has promised me a glass-topped cabinet for Christmas, so that visitors can admire them. Next spring I hope to find a kookaburra's egg, which would make my set complete. Mother says I must not climb the tall trees any more, but I think she is only worried about my good trousers. Your loving nephew, Albert.

encounters.frame: The Thennit is living in an old record sleeve. A very cross letter fell out.
encounters.text: LETTERS TO THE EDITOR, Twotide Times, 3 October 1956. Sir, I must complain about this new 'rock and roll' music that young people have been playing on the radio all year. It is nothing but shouting and banging, and the singers cannot even be bothered to say their words properly. On Saturday night, at the surf club dance, I saw young people throwing each other about the floor in the most dangerous way. One young man spun his partner so fast that she lost a shoe. The noise could be heard as far as the lighthouse, and my cat has not come out from under the bed since. My grandson tells me this music is 'all the rage'. I told him the rage is mine. In my day, we danced the waltz, politely, at arm's length. Several of my neighbours agree with me that this music will never last, and that it is ruining the young people of this island. I ask the surf club to ban it at once. Yours faithfully, Mr E. Grumble, aged 64.

encounters.frame: The Thennit is living in an old glass light bulb. A letter was rolled up inside.
encounters.text: 14 Wattle Street, 18 March 1901. Dear Cousin Bea, The most extraordinary thing happened this week: we have electric light! Two men from the company came on Monday and ran a wire all the way from the pole in the street, through the front window and across the ceiling of the parlour. Now, instead of lighting the lamps, Father simply turns a little brass switch on the wall, and the whole room glows. The first night, we sat up until ten o'clock just looking at it. Half the street came over to see, and Mrs Pomeroy from next door fainted, though Mother says she faints at everything. Grandma refuses to go near the switch. She is convinced that the electricity will leak out of the wire if it is left on, and she makes Father turn it off whenever she is in the room. Mother has kept her box of candles in the kitchen drawer, 'just in case the whole thing is a passing fad'. Only one other family on Wattle Street has electric light so far, and their boy Percy has been boasting about it for weeks. Now we can boast too. Father says that next year we may even have a second light, in the kitchen. Your affectionate cousin, Winifred.

encounters.success: Brand new, rare and astonishing. The letter shows electric light was only just arriving in homes in 1901.

encounters.text: PEMBERTON'S PHOTOGRAPHIC STUDIO, 12 Harbour Street. Established 1884. Have your portrait taken by the finest photographer on the coast! Our studio has a large glass roof, so that we may use the bright light of day, and we are therefore open only when the sun is shining. Sitters must keep perfectly still for one whole minute while the picture is taken. A metal stand will be placed behind your head to help you, and it is quite comfortable once you are used to it. Our assistant, Mr Finch, will dust your face with powder so that it does not shine, and he will hold up a white sheet to bounce the light onto your cheeks. Please do not smile. A serious face looks far more dignified than a grin, and a smile is very difficult to hold for a whole minute. Wear your best clothes for your portrait. Children may hold a favourite toy, provided it does not wriggle. You will not see your picture until it has been printed, two weeks later, on card fit to hang in any parlour. We are very busy on Saturdays, so please book ahead. Mr Pemberton regrets that he can no longer photograph dogs, after the unfortunate incident with the Mayor's poodle.

encounters.frame: Zed found an old computer magazine in a box of cables. The Thennit is living in a cassette tape.
encounters.text: HOME COMPUTING MONTHLY, June 1984. IS THIS THE FUTURE IN YOUR LOUNGE ROOM? This month, we test the brand-new Zephyr 64, one of the first computers small enough and cheap enough for an ordinary family home. Out of the box, it looks rather like a typewriter with no paper, and it plugs into the back of your television set. For readers who have never used one, the keyboard is the part with the letters on it. The Zephyr has a whopping 64 kilobytes of memory, which the makers say is 'more than any family could ever need'. The Zephyr costs about as much as a second-hand car, so most families will need to save for a while. Games are loaded from a cassette tape, and our favourite, Space Moth, took only twelve minutes to load, which is very fast indeed. While you wait, the screen flashes in rainbow stripes and the speaker makes a noise like an angry kettle. Our tester's children played Space Moth for six hours straight, and we are told that one of them has started dreaming in rainbow stripes. Some parents have written to us worrying that home computers will turn children's brains to porridge. We think that is unlikely, but we will report back next month.

encounters.success: One of the first home computers, and twelve minutes counted as fast! Computers were new in 1984.

encounters.frame: The Thennit found an old newspaper wrapped around a tape measure. Mo wrote a note about it, but one word is wrong.
encounters.text: THE COASTAL HERALD, 8 January 1923. INSPECTOR ON PATROL. Beach Inspector Mr Horace Pruitt had a busy weekend at Twotide Beach, where he walked up and down the sand from dawn until dusk with his tape measure. Under the new council rules, every bathing costume must reach from the neck to the knee, and Mr Pruitt measured more than two hundred of them. One elderly gentleman, who had swum at Twotide every morning for forty years, was measured six times on Saturday and complained that his knees were getting cold. Eleven young ladies were sent home because their costumes stopped a full two inches above the knee. A young man was ordered to cover up after he was seen strolling along the water's edge without a top, and he was told that bathing costumes were 'for the water, not for parading about'. When one swimmer pointed out that the rules were old-fashioned, Mr Pruitt replied that he was simply protecting the good name of the beach. 'Decent folk do not want to see knees,' he told our reporter. Several families have written to the council to complain, saying they would rather swim in comfort. The council will discuss the rules again in March. Mr Pruitt has bought a second tape measure, in case the first one wears out.

encounters.frame: The Thennit is living in an old ship's cup. Wren found a letter tucked behind it.
encounters.text: Aboard the RMS Aurelia, 11 April 1912. Dear Mam, We are four days out from port, and this ship is like a floating city, with more than two thousand people on board. I wish you could see it. The first-class passengers have a grand saloon with a glass ceiling, a swimming bath and a band that plays every night. I know this only because I peeked through a door before a steward chased me away. We in third class are not allowed above E deck, and there are locked gates to make sure of it. We eat in our own dining room, down by the engines, where the floor hums and the soup wobbles. Some of the people down here have never seen the sea before, and a boy from our village was sick for the first three days. The food is plain, but there is plenty of it, which is more than we had at home. Yesterday a little girl from first class dropped her ribbon over the rail, and it floated all the way down to our deck. I tied it in my hair. When she saw me from up above, she waved, and I waved back, and her governess pulled her away. Your loving daughter, Rosie.
